idiom_name: plain adapter object over a duck-typed port + mapping module (Forwardable/SimpleDelegator for delegation)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no interfaces to declare, so the port is simply the set of messages the domain sends and the adapter is a plain object answering them, holding the vendor client in an ivar; translation lives in mapping methods on a small module or on the DTO itself (LegacyOrder.from_domain(order)). Delegation where it genuinely applies is a stdlib concern - Forwardable's def_delegator(s) for an explicit member subset, SimpleDelegator when almost everything forwards and only a few messages are translated. What replaces the classic structure is the duck-typed boundary object plus the mapper; the heavier facade/adapter split is justified when the vendor protocol needs its own connection object or the layer fronts several upstream calls.
code_sketch:
class LegacyOrderAdapter          # the domain only sends #place
  def initialize(client) = (@client = client)

  def place(order)
    resp = @client.submit(LegacyOrderMapper.to_legacy(order))  # translate out
    to_receipt(resp)                                           # translate back
  rescue Legacy::RemoteError => e
    raise OrderRejected, e.message                             # error vocabulary
  end
end
pitfalls: method_missing-based forwarding makes the boundary invisible: the vendor API leaks through the object and every typo becomes a runtime NoMethodError.
Never expose the client itself (attr_reader :client) or callers bypass the translation and the layer becomes decorative.
Monkey-patching vendor classes (class Legacy::Order; def to_domain; end) files foreign translation inside the vendor's namespace where nobody looks for it.
Errors from vendor gems live in their own hierarchy; rescue a narrow vendor error and re-raise a domain error with the message preserved.
